name: Uncle John's Tree

location.address: McLaren Lodge, 501 Stanyan Street, Golden Gate Park

verified_sources: https://goldengatepark.substack.com/p/two-christmas-trees (Susan Freinkel, fetched directly: 'Uncle John's Tree... Monterey cypress... Outside McLaren Lodge... planted around 1880; described as one of the oldest in the park')

https://richmondsunsetnews.com/2021/12/02/press-release-tree-lighting-ceremony-in-golden-gate-park-dec-2-2021/ (republished San Francisco Recreation and Park Department press release, fetched directly: 'Known as Uncle John's Tree in honor of Golden Gate Park's designer and first park superintendent John McLaren, the giant cypress was first illuminated with 800 bulbs on McLaren's 84th birthday'; caption confirms location 'at McLaren Lodge in Golden Gate Park')
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLaren_Lodge (coordinates for McLaren Lodge building, fetched directly)
access: Free, always open. Stands on the public lawn immediately outside McLaren Lodge, the SF Recreation and Parks headquarters building at the east end of Golden Gate Park.
transport: MUNI bus lines on Fell/Oak or the N-Judah/5-Fulton corridor stop within a few minutes' walk; the tree stands right at the Panhandle entrance to the park.
verify_notes: Two independent sources: (1) Susan Freinkel's Golden Gate Park history substack, directly fetched, says the Monterey cypress outside McLaren Lodge was planted around 1880, one of the oldest trees in the park. (2) SF Recreation and Park Department's own press release (republished by Richmond Review/Sunset Beacon, directly fetched) confirms the tree stands at McLaren Lodge, is called Uncle John's Tree after park superintendent John McLaren (1846-1943), and has been lit as San Francisco's de facto official Christmas tree since 1929, first lit with 800 bulbs on McLaren's birthday. A third source found via search (SF Examiner, sfrecpark.org, Atlas Obscura) repeats the same 1880s planting and 1929 lighting-tradition facts but those specific pages were blocked (Cloudflare/paywall on sfexaminer and atlasobscura, timeout on sfrecpark.org and goldengatepark.com after two attempts each) so were not used as cited sources, only as corroboration that the two fetched sources are not outliers. Location_precision set approximate: I have the McLaren Lodge building's own coordinates (Wikipedia, 37.7717/-122.4547) and multiple photos/descriptions placing the tree immediately in front of the building's entrance, but no tree-level register coordinate or mapped photo, so the pin is building-level rather than trunk-level. No girth or height measurement found in the sources reached; age is an estimate from the 'planted around 1880' claim (broadened to a 20-year band as a planting-era estimate rather than a precise year) rather than a documented exact planting date, so curation_status is flagged. Remarkable fact for the writer: McLaren asked on his deathbed that the tree keep being lit, and the tradition has continued as San Francisco's closest thing to an official city Christmas tree, illuminated almost every year since 1929.

name: The Landmark Palms of Dolores Street

location.address: Dolores Street median at 730 Dolores Street (between 19th and Liberty Streets)

verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: lists 'Canary Island date palms (Phoenix canariensis), 730 Dolores Street median' and 'Cliff date palms (Phoenix rupicola), 730 Dolores Street median' as two of the city's officially designated Landmark Trees under Article 16 of the Public Works Code)

https://sfstandard.com/2023/01/18/could-sfs-iconic-palm-trees-disappear/ (The San Francisco Standard, fetched directly: 'Those beautiful palms lining Dolores Street? They are Canary Island date palms, beloved enough for the city to officially designate them as trees with landmark status.')
access: Free, always visible from the sidewalk on either side of Dolores Street; the trees stand in the raised median that runs down the centre of the street, so they are seen rather than walked among.
transport: J-Church Muni Metro runs the length of Dolores Street; the 33 and 24 bus lines cross it nearby. Street parking and a wide sidewalk on both sides.
verify_notes: Two independent directly-fetched sources confirm existence and official Landmark Tree status: the city's own Landmark Tree Program list (sfenvironment.org) names both the Canary Island date palms AND a pair of rarer Cliff Date Palms (Phoenix rupicola) at this exact location, '730 Dolores Street median', among its 25-ish citywide landmark designations; the SF Standard (2023) independently corroborates that the Dolores Street palms specifically are Canary Island date palms with official landmark status. Dolores Street's median carries roughly 199 palms in total running much of the street's length (per a widely repeated but not directly verified figure), so this entry is deliberately scoped to the single specific block the city register names, not the whole avenue, to keep it one collectible, findable point rather than an unbounded row. That block is also distinguished by holding the two rare Cliff Date Palms alongside the more common Canary Island palms, which is presumably why the city singled it out. AGE NOT ESTABLISHED from a directly-fetched source: a PalmTalk forum thread titled '1910 San Francisco Dolores Street Canary Date Palms' and an ASLA project page (found via search summary only, not fetched, so not used as evidence per the search-summary-is-a-lead rule) suggest the palms date to the street's post-1906-earthquake rebuilding and were planted in stages from the 1920s, which is plausible (Canary Island date palms are extremely slow-growing and full-size specimens like these typically take many decades) but unconfirmed by a source I actually read. Leave age_estimate empty and let the page ask the reader or a later pass with time to read the historical photo archive properly. location_precision confirmed because the register itself names this exact median block by street address, which is as precise as a linear median feature gets; a visitor stands on either sidewalk and sees exactly this planting.

access: Free, always open. Stands at the top of a public hillside stairway garden in the street's own public right-of-way, tended by the neighbourhood association with city (SFDPW) support; not on private land at any point.

Cork oak (Quercus suber) is a Mediterranean species grown for its thick, harvestable bark, an unusual planting for a residential SF hillside. No age, girth or planting date found in either source. verified_sources: https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (San Francisco Department of the Environment, official Landmark Tree list, fetched directly: 'Moreton Bay fig (Ficus macrophylla), 3555 Cesar Chavez Street')

access: Free, always visible from the public sidewalk on Valencia Street; stands on hospital grounds fronting the street rather than inside a fenced garden.
transport: On Valencia Street at Cesar Chavez, in the Mission/Bernal Heights border; the 14, 49 and 67 Muni bus lines all pass within a couple of blocks.
verify_notes: Three independent directly-fetched sources agree: the city's official Landmark Tree list gives the address 3555 Cesar Chavez Street; Mike Sullivan's published-book-backed tree site places it more precisely on Valencia Street just south of Cesar Chavez, west side, by the hospital, calling it 'a very large specimen'; a local history blog (Burrito Justice) independently calls it 'the huge Moreton Bay fig in front of St. Luke's on Valencia' and confirms landmark status, noting it recently lost a branch. Search-summary-only findings (not used as sourced facts, only as corroboration): landmarked by Mayor Gavin Newsom in March 2008; described elsewhere as the largest Moreton Bay fig specimen in San Francisco, a species otherwise rare this far north (it is much more common in Southern California). Moreton Bay fig is a genuinely spectacular species: a banyan-like Australian native capable of huge buttressed, spreading crowns; famous specimens exist in LA, Santa Barbara and San Diego's Balboa Park, and this is San Francisco's own large example. No age, girth or planting date found in the fetched sources. Location precision is approximate: I have the hospital's own address coordinates and a directly-fetched description narrowing it to 'Valencia Street south of Cesar Chavez, west side', which is a short block frontage, but no exact tree-level coordinate or mapped photo.
